keyIdea.text: Fabric CA issues X.509 certificates and manages identity lifecycle for peers, orderers, clients and admins. Its hierarchical PKI enables safer operations by isolating root trust from daily issuance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Introduction
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
An operational walkthrough and CLI demo for secure identity issuance.

Fabric CA: issuing trusted identities

Fabric CA is the Hyperledger project CA server that issues X.509 certificates for every network entity. It supports hierarchical PKI, registration and enrollment flows, and CLI tooling for administrators.

In this lesson

Root vs Intermediate, register and enroll, server config, CLI demo.

Security focus

Protect the CA private key; consider HSMs in production.

Hands-on

Start a CA server and perform enroll/register commands.

Concept map
trust hierarchy
Root CA
Self-signed trust anchor. Keep offline and highly protected.
Intermediate CA
Operational CA that issues certificates to peers, orderers, and users.
Registration
Creates an identity record with an enrollment ID and secret; no certificate yet.
Enrollment
Entity generates a key and CSR, then retrieves a signed certificate from the CA.
Key Takeaway

Fabric CA is central to identity and trust in Fabric. Use a Root CA as an offline anchor and Intermediate CAs for operational issuance to reduce blast radius.

Second, you will learn to distinguish a Root CA from an Intermediate CA, including the security trade-offs and when to keep a root offline. Third, you will explain registration and enrollment as two distinct lifecycle steps: registration creates a record and a secret, while enrollment uses that secret to obtain a signed certificate. Fourth, you will gain the ability to configure basic server parameters such as the database backend, listening port, signing profiles, and the CA identity. Each skill includes a short mnemonic or visual to help you remember the lifecycle flow and the role separation. These competencies prepare you to perform CLI tasks like starting a CA server, enrolling a bootstrap admin, and registering new identities in a secure, repeatable way.

screens.title: Who receives certificates from Fabric CA?
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric CA issues X.509 certificates to every participant that needs identity and crypto material: organizational entities, peer nodes, orderer nodes, administrative users, and client applications. This means each peer and orderer has a certificate used for TLS and mutual authentication, and client applications use certificates to sign transactions and to authenticate to peers and orderers. Importantly, organizations typically operate their own Fabric CA instance. Running per-organization CAs preserves sovereign control over membership and allows a consortium to decentralize trust. For example, Org1 runs its CA and issues certificates to its peers and apps; Org2 keeps its own CA for its members. This separation prevents a single CA compromise from affecting every organization and supports governance where each organization can set policies for its own identities. A common misconception is that a single central CA is simpler; while true operationally, it creates a single point of failure and complicates trust boundaries in a consortium. The practical takeaway is: plan CA placement by organizational boundaries, and design your certificate issuance processes so that a compromised CA only affects a limited scope of identities. How would you partition CAs in your consortium to minimize operational blast radius?

keyIdea.title: Per-org CA model
keyIdea.text: Each organization typically runs its own Fabric CA to maintain sovereign identity control and reduce cross-organization risk.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Who gets certificates
Core Concept

Recipients and ownership

Peers, orderers, client applications and administrators all require X.509 credentials issued by a CA. Ownership of the CA normally maps to organizational boundaries for governance and security.

Example: peer identity
A peer uses its certificate for TLS and for signing transactions during endorsement.
Misconception
Using a single central CA may simplify setup but increases the blast radius if keys are compromised.
Key Takeaway

Map CA ownership to organizational trust boundaries to reduce risk and maintain governance autonomy.

Comparison: Single CA vs Per-Org CAs
Single central CA
  • Simple to run initially.
  • Single point of failure across consortium.
  • Harder to enforce per-org policy boundaries.
Per-organization CAs
  • Decentralized control and clear ownership.
  • Limits impact of a CA compromise to that organization.
  • Supports independent policy and auditing.
Concrete scenario
Org1 runs a CA that issues certificates for org1 peers and apps. If Org1's intermediate CA is compromised, Org2's identities remain unaffected because Org2 manages its own CA.

screens.title: Root CA and Intermediate CA
screens.narratorSegment: A Root CA is the ultimate trust anchor in a hierarchical PKI. Its certificate is self-signed and everything else in the hierarchy traces trust back to it. Because it is so sensitive, best practice is to keep the Root CA offline and tightly secured. An Intermediate CA receives a certificate signed by the Root CA and performs day-to-day certificate issuance for peers, orderers, and users. This separation of responsibilities reduces the operational risk: if an Intermediate CA private key is compromised, only the certificates it issued are affected. You would then use the Root CA to sign a new Intermediate CA certificate and restore operations with limited disruption. The concrete example to bear in mind is: keep the Root CA in a protected, offline environment and run one or more Intermediate CAs in a hardened online environment for certificate issuance. A common misconception is that more intermediates always add complexity without benefit; in fact, careful use of intermediates gives you the ability to revoke, rotate, and constrain issuance scope without touching the Root CA. Consider: what processes would you put in place for rotating an Intermediate CA in your deployment?

keyIdea.text: Keep the Root CA offline as the trust anchor and use Intermediate CAs for operational issuance to limit blast radius and enable rotation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Root vs Intermediate
Definition

Root CA and Intermediate CA

Root CA: self-signed trust anchor. Intermediate CA: signed by root and used for routine issuance.

Security practice
Keep the Root CA offline and very restricted. Use intermediates for online issuance to limit compromise impact.
Operational benefit
If an intermediate is compromised, the root can sign a replacement intermediate without rebuilding the entire PKI.
Key Takeaway

Structure PKI so operational keys are separate from the offline root to enable safe rotation and recovery.

Hierarchy diagram
Root CA (offline)
Self-signed certificate. Highest trust anchor.
Signs
Intermediate CA A
Issues certs for Org1 peers and clients.
Intermediate CA B
Issues certs for Org2 peers and clients.
If one intermediate is compromised, revoke its certificates and create a new intermediate signed by the root.

screens.title: Registration: creating an identity record
screens.narratorSegment: Registration creates an identity record in the Fabric CA server's database. It does not issue a certificate. When you register an identity you specify an enrollment ID, a secret password, the identity type like peer, orderer, client, or admin, its affiliation path such as org1. department1, and any attributes that influence permissions. The registration prepares the CA to accept an enrollment request later. A practical example: registering a client named appuser1 with a secret called appuser1pw and assigning it to org1. department1. The concrete command from the chapter shows the typical flags you will use with fabric-ca-client register. After running the register command, the CA stores the entry and you can hand the secret to the entity that will later enroll. A common mistake is to treat registration as enrollment — remember registration only creates credentials in the CA database. Another frequent error is hardcoding secrets or failing to rotate them after first use. For practice: register a user with limited attributes and then require rotating the secret immediately after the first enrollment to reduce exposure. Registration: creating an identity record means registration creates a record with an enrollment id, secret, type, affiliation and attributes; it does not issue certificates.. In practical terms, what registration stores and a concrete register command. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Registration
Process Flow

Registering an identity

Registration adds the enrollment ID and secret to the CA database and sets its type, affiliation and attributes.

Common fields
  • enrollment ID and secret
  • type: peer, orderer, client, admin
  • affiliation: org1.department1
  • attributes: hf.Registrar.Roles, hf.Revoker, etc.
Misconception
Registration does not provide certificates. Enrollment is required to obtain certs and keys.
Example action

Register appuser1 with a secret and affiliation so it can later enroll for a certificate.

CLI example
# Assuming you are authenticated as an admin with the Fabric CA server
fabric-ca-client register --id.name appuser1 --id.secret appuser1pw --id.type client --id.affiliation org1.department1 --id.attrs 'hf.Registrar.Roles=client,hf.Registrar.DelegateRoles=client,hf.Revoker=true,hf.IntermediateCA=true'
After this command the CA database contains an entry for appuser1 and the secret appuser1pw which is later used to enroll.
Check your understanding
Why should enrollment secrets be rotated or deleted after initial use? What happens if a secret is exposed?

screens.title: Enrollment: obtaining certificates and keys
screens.narratorSegment: Enrollment is the step where an identity uses its enrollment ID and secret to request and receive an X.509 certificate and the corresponding private key. Crucially, the entity generates its private key locally and creates a Certificate Signing Request, which contains the public key and identity details like the common name and host names. The enrollment command sends the CSR plus the enrollment credentials to the Fabric CA. The CA verifies the supplied enrollment ID and secret against its registration records, signs the CSR, and returns the X.509 certificate and, optionally, the CA certificate chain. The result is an MSP directory containing the certificate, private key, and necessary CA chain files so that Fabric components recognize the identity. For example, enrolling appuser1 with its secret stores the MSP materials in the directory specified by the -M flag. A misconception to avoid: do not let private keys be generated on the CA; that breaks key ownership guarantees. Always generate private keys on the client or node and transfer only public CSRs to the CA. Enrollment: obtaining certificates and keys means enrollment uses a locally generated key and csr plus the enrollment secret to obtain a signed x.509 certificate and msp materials for the identity.. In practical terms, csr generation, verification and msp material. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Enrollment uses a locally generated key and CSR plus the enrollment secret to obtain a signed X.509 certificate and MSP materials for the identity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Enrollment
Process Flow

Enroll to obtain certificates

The entity generates a private key locally, creates a CSR, and uses the enrollment ID and secret to request a signed certificate from the CA.

  • Generate private key locally — ownership never leaves the entity.
  • Create CSR including common name and hosts.
  • Use fabric-ca-client enroll with credentials; receive certificate and CA chain.
  • Store MSP in the directory provided by the -M flag.
Misconception
Never generate persistent private keys on the CA. Keys should be under the control of the node or client.
CLI example
# To enroll appuser1 after registration
fabric-ca-client enroll -u https://appuser1:appuser1pw@localhost:7054 --csr.cn appuser1 --csr.hosts 'appuser1.org1.example.com' -M /path/to/enrollment/msp
The -M flag sets where the MSP material, including the certificate and private key, will be stored.
Example result
You will find the signcerts, keystore, and cacerts files inside the MSP directory, which Fabric uses to identify the entity.
Key Takeaway

Enrollment issues the certificate based on a locally created key and CSR. Keep key ownership at the client or node and secure enrollment secrets.

screens.title: fabric-ca-client flags and MSP storage
screens.narratorSegment: The fabric-ca-client is the CLI you will use to register and enroll identities. For registration you supply flags such as the enrollment ID, secret, type, affiliation and attributes. For enrollment you typically use an -u URL that includes the enrollment ID and secret and optionally a TLS certificate file. The CSR flags let you set the certificate common name and host names that will appear in the certificate. The -M flag is important because it determines where the generated MSP materials — the certificate, private key, and CA chain — are stored on disk. For example, when you enroll an admin you might set FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME to a temporary directory so the generated MSP is isolated, then copy the necessary files into your node's configuration. A common mistake is to forget to point -M at a secure directory or to store generated keys in an unsecured location. Another pitfall is confusing registration attributes with enrollment parameters; attributes are recorded at registration and referenced during enrollment checks. Practice by enrolling a client to a test directory, inspecting the signcerts and keystore files, and confirming the cacerts chain is present.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › CLI flags & MSP
Code Walkthrough

Key flags and their meaning

  • -u: the enrollment URL that includes the enrollment ID and secret for enrollment requests.
  • --csr.cn and --csr.hosts: set the certificate common name and DNS/host SANs.
  • -M: directory where MSP material is written after enroll.
Practical tip
Set FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME and use isolated folders for enrollments to avoid accidentally mixing MSP materials between identities.
Example enroll and MSP layout
fabric-ca-client enroll -u https://appuser1:appuser1pw@localhost:7054 --csr.cn appuser1 --csr.hosts 'appuser1.org1.example.com' -M /path/to/enrollment/msp

# After enrollment, MSP directory contains:
# /path/to/enrollment/msp/signcerts/
# /path/to/enrollment/msp/keystore/
# /path/to/enrollment/msp/cacerts/
Inspect these folders to confirm the certificate, private key, and CA chain are present. Incorrect placement or permissions can prevent Fabric from recognizing the identity.

screens.title: Fabric CA server configuration
screens.narratorSegment: The Fabric CA server is driven by a configuration file, typically named fabric-ca-server-config. yaml. Key parameters include the database configuration — you can use lightweight SQLite for testing or PostgreSQL for production — and the listening port the server uses to accept requests. Signing profiles control certificate validity periods and key usages, shaping the certificates the CA issues. The ca section defines the server's own identity, including the private key and certificate it uses to sign issued certificates. For a Root CA the certificate is self-signed; for an Intermediate CA the server operates with a certificate signed by its parent. Properly configuring these parameters ensures certificates have appropriate lifetimes and are usable for expected purposes like TLS and enrollment. A common misconfiguration is leaving default signing profiles that are too permissive or not setting a durable database backend for production. Always ensure private key paths are protected and that the CA's storage volume is backed up securely. Think about which signing profiles you need for client certificates versus TLS certificates and configure them explicitly in production. Fabric CA server configuration means configure the db, listening port, signing profiles, and ca identity in the yaml file, and protect ca keys and storage in production.. In practical terms, essential parameters in fabric-ca-server-config.yaml. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Server configuration
Definition

fabric-ca-server-config.yaml essentials

Control where the CA stores data, how it signs certificates, and the identity it presents to clients.

Database
Choose SQLite for test setups, PostgreSQL for production durability and concurrency.
Listening port
Configure the port the CA will serve on and set TLS if required.
Signing profiles

screens.title: Enrolling the bootstrap administrator
screens.narratorSegment: After starting the CA server with a bootstrap admin, you must enroll that admin to obtain its MSP so it can perform registrations. Enrolling the bootstrap admin creates an MSP directory that contains the admin certificate and key. The environment variable FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME is commonly set to isolate the client's local working directory and to store the admin MSP material there. A practical pattern is to create a temporary admin-msp folder, enroll the admin into that folder, and then use those credentials to register additional users. For example, you would set FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME to./admin-msp, run fabric-ca-client enroll with the bootstrap credentials, and ensure the CA certificate is available to the client with the --tls. certfiles flag. Definition

Admin enrollment and client home

Use FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME to control where the client stores MSP materials. Enroll the bootstrap admin to prepare for registering new users.

Practical step
Set FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME to a clean directory like admin-msp, copy or reference the CA certificate, then run fabric-ca-client enroll for the admin.

screens.title: Attributes, affiliations, and registrar controls
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric CA supports fine-grained control over who can register and enroll which identities. Affiliations are hierarchical paths like org1. department1 used to group identities and apply policies. Attributes are name-value pairs attached to a registered identity and control capabilities. Two important attributes are hf. Registrar. Roles and hf. Registrar. DelegateRoles. hf. Registrar. Roles defines the types of identities an enrolled registrar is permitted to register or enroll for, such as client or peer. hf. Registrar. DelegateRoles defines which identity types that registrar is allowed to delegate registration for, meaning they can create new registrars with those roles. A concrete example: during registration you might set hf. Registrar. Roles=client to allow a registrar to create client identities only. A common pitfall is confusing these two: giving DelegateRoles too broadly lets a registrar create other registrars with wide permissions. Plan attributes carefully and give the least privilege necessary for the role. Also confirm affiliation paths match your organizational structure to simplify auditing and policy enforcement. Attributes, affiliations, and registrar controls means use affiliations to group identities and attributes like hf.registrar.roles and hf.registrar.delegateroles to enforce least privilege when delegating registration.. Affiliations and attributes

Affiliations group identities by org and unit. Attributes control registrar permissions and other identity metadata.

hf.Registrar.Roles
Specifies identity types the registrar may create or enroll, such as client, peer, or orderer.

screens.title: Security best practices for Fabric CA
screens.narratorSegment: The CA's private key is the master key for issuing identities. If it is compromised, an attacker could issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate network participants. Therefore, protecting the CA private key is paramount. For a Root CA, keep the key offline and under strict access controls. For Intermediate CAs, consider using Hardware Security Modules to store keys in production. Avoid hardcoding enrollment secrets and delete or rotate them after enrollment to reduce exposure. Regularly back up CA configuration and cryptographic material but encrypt backups and restrict access. Plan recovery and rotation processes: if an Intermediate CA key is compromised, revoke its issued certificates where possible and issue a new intermediate certificate signed by the Root CA. A common mistake is failing to test recovery processes; running tabletop drills or staging a key rotation ensures that you can restore trust with minimal downtime. Finally, audit CA operations and regularly review attributes and affiliations to confirm only intended identities can register and enroll. Security best practices for Fabric CA means secure ca private keys with strict access controls, consider hsms for production, rotate secrets, and have tested recovery processes for compromised intermediates.. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Security Best Practices
Core Concept

Protecting CA material

Treat the CA private key as the most sensitive secret. Use hardware protection and strict controls.

Offline root
Keep Root CA offline where possible to minimize exposure.
Use HSMs
Consider Hardware Security Modules for private key storage in production.
Secrets lifecycle
Avoid hardcoding, rotate secrets, and remove them after initial use.
Recovery and rotation
If an intermediate is compromised, revoke its certs and sign a replacement intermediate with the root. Test your recovery procedures before production.
Audit & access
Enable logging and audit CA operations. Restrict who can read the CA private key and database backups.
Common mistake

Not testing key rotation and recovery leads to long outages and uncertain trust repairs.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: start CA, enroll admin, register a user
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough ties together the previous screens into a short lab sequence. First, prepare a directory to hold CA data. Next, set FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME to a temporary admin-msp folder and enroll the bootstrap admin using the enrollment URL and the CA certificate for TLS verification. Step-by-step commands
mkdir -p ca-data
cd ca-data

docker run -d --name fabric-ca-server -p 7054:7054 \
  -e FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME=/etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server \

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what role a Fabric Certificate Authority plays in a multi-organization Fabric network and why it matters for secure identity management. Fabric CA issues X.509 certificates to organizations, peers, orderers, client applications, and administrators so every participant can authenticate and transact securely. You will see how organizations often run their own CA instance, why a hierarchical PKI with Root and Intermediate CAs reduces operational risk, and how the two-step lifecycle of registration and enrollment produces usable cryptographic identities. I will also walk you through the essential CLI actions you will use during onboarding: starting a CA server, enrolling a bootstrap administrator, registering an identity, and enrolling that identity to produce an MSP directory. A concrete example we will use throughout is creating a Root CA, generating an Intermediate CA for day-to-day issuance, then registering and enrolling a client application so it can interact with peers. Finally, we'll cover common mistakes, like leaving enrollment secrets exposed or failing to secure the CA private key, and how those errors compromise trust. By the end you will understand the practical steps and the security trade-offs when operating Fabric CAs.

These objectives map to practical competencies you need to operate Fabric CAs safely. First, you will be able to identify Fabric CA's role and why each organization commonly runs its own CA instance; this matters because decentralized identity control is core to consortium governance. Second, you will learn to distinguish a Root CA from an Intermediate CA, including the security trade-offs and when to keep a root offline. Third, you will explain registration and enrollment as two distinct lifecycle steps: registration creates a record and a secret, while enrollment uses that secret to obtain a signed certificate. Fourth, you will gain the ability to configure basic server parameters such as the database backend, listening port, signing profiles, and the CA identity. Each skill includes a short mnemonic or visual to help you remember the lifecycle flow and the role separation. These competencies prepare you to perform CLI tasks like starting a CA server, enrolling a bootstrap admin, and registering new identities in a secure, repeatable way.

These additional objectives focus on practical skills you'll use every day when running Fabric CAs. First, you will learn to start and interact with a Fabric CA server using the official CLI, which is essential for bootstrapping administrators and performing registrations. Second, you will understand how enrollment MSP material is stored on disk and why the MSP directory matters for node and client identity recognition in Fabric. Third, you will manage attributes and affiliations; Fabric CA uses affiliation paths to group identities and attributes to control registrar permissions. Fourth, you will adopt security best practices such as protecting enrollment secrets, rotating compromised keys, and considering hardware security modules for CA private key storage. Each objective ties to a verification milestone so you can prove competency in a lab or exam scenario.

Fabric CA issues X.509 certificates to every participant that needs identity and crypto material: organizational entities, peer nodes, orderer nodes, administrative users, and client applications. This means each peer and orderer has a certificate used for TLS and mutual authentication, and client applications use certificates to sign transactions and to authenticate to peers and orderers. Importantly, organizations typically operate their own Fabric CA instance. Running per-organization CAs preserves sovereign control over membership and allows a consortium to decentralize trust. For example, Org1 runs its CA and issues certificates to its peers and apps; Org2 keeps its own CA for its members. This separation prevents a single CA compromise from affecting every organization and supports governance where each organization can set policies for its own identities. A common misconception is that a single central CA is simpler; while true operationally, it creates a single point of failure and complicates trust boundaries in a consortium. The practical takeaway is: plan CA placement by organizational boundaries, and design your certificate issuance processes so that a compromised CA only affects a limited scope of identities. How would you partition CAs in your consortium to minimize operational blast radius?

A Root CA is the ultimate trust anchor in a hierarchical PKI. Its certificate is self-signed and everything else in the hierarchy traces trust back to it. Because it is so sensitive, best practice is to keep the Root CA offline and tightly secured. An Intermediate CA receives a certificate signed by the Root CA and performs day-to-day certificate issuance for peers, orderers, and users. This separation of responsibilities reduces the operational risk: if an Intermediate CA private key is compromised, only the certificates it issued are affected. You would then use the Root CA to sign a new Intermediate CA certificate and restore operations with limited disruption. The concrete example to bear in mind is: keep the Root CA in a protected, offline environment and run one or more Intermediate CAs in a hardened online environment for certificate issuance. A common misconception is that more intermediates always add complexity without benefit; in fact, careful use of intermediates gives you the ability to revoke, rotate, and constrain issuance scope without touching the Root CA. Enrollment is the step where an identity uses its enrollment ID and secret to request and receive an X.509 certificate and the corresponding private key. The enrollment command sends the CSR plus the enrollment credentials to the Fabric CA. The CA verifies the supplied enrollment ID and secret against its registration records, signs the CSR, and returns the X.509 certificate and, optionally, the CA certificate chain. The result is an MSP directory containing the certificate, private key, and necessary CA chain files so that Fabric components recognize the identity.
